title: Spread spectrum, keying defects and digital codes
blurb: How spread spectrum resists interference, why key clicks and overmodulation happen, and how Baudot, ASCII and parity differ.

E8D01.why: The receiver correlates with the spreading pattern, so signals **not using that algorithm are suppressed**.
E8D01.trap: Resistance comes from the spreading pattern, not from high power or feedback.

E8D02.why: **Direct sequence** uses a high-speed bit stream to shift the carrier's phase.

E8D03.why: **Frequency hopping** varies the transmitted frequency rapidly in a pseudorandom sequence.
E8D03.trap: Shifting the phase with a fast bit stream describes direct sequence.

E8D04.why: Extremely short rise and fall times make abrupt keying edges, which **generate key clicks**.
E8D04.trap: Clicks are broadband sideband splatter from the keying edges, not harmonics.

E8D05.why: Softening the keying edges is the usual cure: **increase rise and fall times**.
E8D05.trap: Shortening the edges makes clicks worse.

E8D06.why: A parity bit makes the count of ones even or odd, so **some errors can be detected**. It adds a bit and corrects nothing.
E8D06.trap: Parity adds overhead, so it slows the rate slightly rather than speeding it.

E8D07.why: Too much audio drive overmodulates AFSK: **excessive transmit audio levels**.
E8D07.trap: Retries and modem bit errors are results of bad signals, not causes of overmodulation.

E8D08.why: Overdriven audio creates unwanted products, measured as **intermodulation distortion (IMD)**.

E8D09.why: Acceptable IMD for an idling PSK signal is **−30 dB** (relative to the signal) or lower.
E8D09.trap: Positive dB values would mean the distortion is stronger than the signal.

E8D10.why: Baudot: **5 data bits**, plus **two shift codes** (letters and figures). ASCII: 7 or 8 bits and no shift codes.

E8D11.why: ASCII has both cases, so you can **send uppercase and lowercase text**. Baudot has only one case.
E8D11.trap: ASCII has no built-in error correction, and it uses more bits than Baudot.
